title: Financial Advisor Reviews: SEC and State Rules Explained
summary: Reviews can boost your business profile, but some states prohibit financial advisor reviews for marketing purposes.
body_markdown:
Client reviews and[testimonials](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/financial-advisor-testimonials) can underscore your credibility as an advisor and help attract new prospects to your firm. The SEC’s marketing rule permits the use of financial advisor reviews in marketing materials, with some stipulations. However, individual states may restrict or prohibit the use of reviews for promotional purposes. Reviewing the latest guidelines for your state can ensure compliance with marketing regulations.

## Financial Advisor Reviews: SEC vs. State Rules


The[SEC’s marketing rule](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/sec-marketing-rule-faqs) , which took effect in 2021, allows advisors to use reviews and testimonials in marketing materials. This includes reviews from clients as well as endorsements from non-clients, such as centers of influence or industry professionals. These rules apply to SEC-registered investment advisors.


Recognizing the need for alignment with SEC standards, the North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA) proposed a rule change that would allow state-registered advisors to use testimonials, endorsements and specific performance reporting within a compliant framework. In May 2026, NASAA voted to pass the amendments but individual states can decide whether to adopt the new rules.1


As of November 2026, 11 states explicitly prohibited smaller advisory firms from publishing client reviews while allowing it for larger firms, according to research from Wealthtender. For the purposes of Wealthtender’s research, “small” means a state-registered firm while “large” means SEC-registered.2 Another 10 states have laws on the books prohibiting reviews, but have agreed to grant leeway to advisors in light of the NASAA amendments or are likely to adopt the new rules. Other states are tentatively or actively moving toward adoption.

## Compliance Rules for Financial Advisor Reviews


If you’re[SEC-registered](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/registering-with-the-sec) or registered in a state that follows the SEC’s marketing rule, you can use reviews, endorsements and testimonials to market your business, but you must do so compliantly. Here’s what’s required:


### Disclosures


Financial advisors who use testimonials or endorsements in their marketing must provide information about the reviewer’s relationship with the firm. This includes identifying whether the person is a current client or non-client, disclosing any cash or noncash compensation they received and describing any material[conflicts of interest](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/how-to-disclose-conflicts-of-interest-as-a-financial-advisor) tied to the relationship or compensation.


Certain disclosures must be clear and prominent so prospective clients can easily find them. Concealing required information behind hyperlinks or displaying it in small, difficult-to-read text may violate the SEC’s marketing rule.


### Written Agreements


If an advisor pays a promoter more than $1,000 over a rolling 12-month period for reviews or testimonials, there must be a written agreement in place detailing the arrangement. Written agreements are generally not required for[compliance](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/sec-compliance) for affiliated personnel when the relationship is clear or has already been disclosed.


### Ineligible Persons


The SEC’s marketing rule restricts advisors from compensating certain individuals for testimonials or endorsements if they have a history of specified disciplinary actions or other disqualifying events. Advisors must take reasonable steps to determine whether a compensated promoter is eligible, although exceptions apply in certain circumstances.


### Third-Party Reviews and Ratings


Advisors may also use reviews from third-party websites in their marketing, assuming they comply with applicable testimonial and endorsement requirements. The SEC has separate rules for third-party ratings, such as rankings or scores issued by independent organizations.


When advertising a third-party rating, advisors generally must disclose when the rating was issued, the period it covers, who created it and whether the advisor paid to obtain or use it. Advisors should also have reason to believe that the rating was based on a survey that didn’t favor positive reviews or discourage negative feedback.


### Other Compliance Requirements


The marketing rule bars advisors from making any false or misleading statements in their marketing materials. They can’t include any unsubstantiated claims, including claims made in reviews, without providing evidence to back them up. Advisors must give all of their clients an opportunity to share a review; cherry-picking is not allowed and negative reviews can’t be deleted or ignored.


SEC-registered advisors must report certain marketing activities, including their use of testimonials, endorsements and third-party ratings, on[Form ADV](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/annual-updating-amendment-to-form-adv) . They must also maintain records of advertisements they disseminate, including client testimonials used in those materials. These records generally must be retained for at least five years, measured from the end of the fiscal year in which the advertisement was last disseminated.


## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)


**How Can Advisors Ask Clients for Reviews?**


Advisors can request reviews through individual conversations, emails or other outreach methods, provided they follow applicable marketing regulations. Soliciting feedback from all clients or a consistently defined group can help avoid concerns about selectively requesting positive testimonials. Advisors should encourage honest feedback without influencing what clients say and maintain records consistent with their firm’s compliance policies.


**How Can Advisors Deal With Negative Reviews?**


Advisors who receive a negative review online should document the review and share it with their[chief compliance officer (CCO)](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/what-does-a-chief-compliance-officer-do) . That includes capturing screenshots of the review itself, along with the reviewer’s publicly-listed information. The next step is determining whether the reviewer is a current, former or non-client. The CCO may direct the advisor to reach out to the reviewer to find a resolution; any communications must be properly archived. If the advisor opts not to reach out, asking all current clients to share reviews may help to offset the negative if they only have good things to say about the business.


**Can Client Reviews Boost an Advisor Marketing Strategy?**


Earning positive reviews from current clients can underscore your brand’s credibility and potentially help increase visibility among prospects. Reviews, whether they’re located on your website or a third-party platform, can tell prospects a little about what it’s like to work with you and what they can expect should they decide to become your client.


## Bottom Line


Financial advisor reviews can strengthen your marketing but it’s important to adhere to compliance rules when using them. If you’re a state registered advisor who is currently prohibited from leveraging reviews or testimonials, consider how you can fill the gap elsewhere in your marketing plan. For example, developing a[thought leadership strategy](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/financial-services-thought-leadership) or hosting educational seminars could raise your profile among the ideal clients you hope to target.
